title: Slack Farm (15Un28), Union County
summary: In Union County, Slack Farm was a large Caborn-Welborn Mississippian village of about 75 acres, occupied from about 1400 to 1700 CE.
bodyMarkdown:
In the fall of 1987, the Kentucky Heritage Council learned that people were looting a village site in Union County. Ten men had leased the right to dig there. They tore open hundreds of graves to search for pots and beads to sell. The damage horrified people across the country, and Slack Farm became a turning point in how the United States protects Native graves.

The village had a long history before that. Slack Farm was a large community of the [Caborn-Welborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caborn-Welborn_culture) culture, a late [Mississippian](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mississippian_culture) people of the lower Ohio Valley, occupied from about 1400 to 1700 CE. Sidney S. Lyon recorded it for the Smithsonian Institution in 1868, but it got little professional attention after that until the looting.

It covered about 75 acres. At least seven residential areas each had their own storage pits and cemeteries. Six were grouped around a plaza or a series of courtyards, and graves were often laid out in parallel rows facing the plaza. Houses were shallow basins with [wattle-and-daub](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wattle_and_daub) walls, made of woven wooden strips plastered with clay.

Each house had a clay hearth. When families left a house, they broke their old cooking and serving pots and left them in the hearth. Storage pits more than six feet wide and six feet deep held dried food. Some had sprouted corn, a sign that part of the stored crop had spoiled.

One full pit may have fed seven to twelve people for a year. Jars carried trailed and incised triangles that archaeologists read as sun symbols.

Slack Farm was connected to faraway places. [Catlinite](https://grokipedia.com/page/Catlinite) and non-local pottery came from the north. Central Mississippi Valley pots, Nodena arrowheads and marine shell came from the southwest. After about 1550, glass beads and ornaments cut from European copper and brass kettles arrived through Native trade networks, before any European is known to have visited.

In early 1988, archaeologists from the Heritage Council, the University of Kentucky and Indiana University, along with several hundred volunteers, documented more than 450 looter holes. They recorded more than 300 burials in seven cemetery areas. Forensic study found the looters had disturbed at least 850 people. Those remains were then reburied at the site.

## Kentucky today

Public outrage over Slack Farm helped push Kentucky and other states to strengthen their grave-protection laws. It also helped build support for the federal [Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act](https://grokipedia.com/page/Native_American_Graves_Protection_and_Repatriation_Act) of 1990. The site is protected, and its location stays off public maps. Union County's lesson is simple: these are graves, not treasure.
Source: [https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Slack-Farm.aspx](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Slack-Farm.aspx)
